newsitem.title: PERU: Government, rebels in Peru wage psychological war.
newsitem.headline: Government, rebels in Peru wage psychological war.

text.p: Eleven days into the Peruvian hostage crisis, President Alberto Fujimori's government and the Marxist guerrillas holding 103 VIPs have intensified their use of psychological warfare to wear each other down.

In the past few days, a spate of statements purporting to come from the guerrillas, selective leaks to the media by security forces and dubious published allegations have created a climate in which, diplomats say, very little can be taken at face value.
"Each side tries to unsettle the other with methods of black propaganda," one diplomat said.

Guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the residence of the Japanese ambassador on Dec. 17 during a glittering reception and took more than 500 diplomats, businessmen and government officials hostage. All but 103 have been released.

In the latest of several media appearances by guerrilla spokesmen whose authenticity is far from certain, a hooded man identifying himself as Commandante Santana said in a television interview from New York that the residence would be blown up on New Year's Day unless Fujimori agreed to the rebels' demands.
"We will execute all the hostages on January 1," he said, unless the government complied with the demands.
Fujimori has refused to release 400 Tupac Amaru guerrillas serving long terms in Peruvian prisons. On Friday he won backing from home and abroad for his tough stand.

In another shot in the guerrillas' war of words, a rambling communique purporting to come from an MRTA "battalion" charged the government with corrupting the system of justice, being complicit in drug-trafficking and abusing its power.

Unusually for a communique from a Marxist-oriented group, it quoted extensive passages from the Bible to back up its contentions. And it added that no further hostages would be released unless the foreign press published the full text.

While guerrilla statements have castigated the government for alleged repression and for failing to improve the lot of the poor majority in Peru, the government has painted the hostage-takers as barbarians.

Earlier in the week, the pro-government newspaper Expreso reported that the 103 hostages were being subjected to psychological torture, with rebels pressing pistols to their necks and then pulling the triggers -- on empty chambers.
The Red Cross, whose representatives are acting as go-betweens in the government-guerrilla standoff, promptly said there was nothing to the claim.
Apparently to keep up pressure on the 20-odd guerrillas inside the elegant residence, security sources have leaked details of high-level overflights by a U.S.-made spy plane.
On Saturday the mass-circulation newspaper La Republica devoted two entire pages to special-operations forces it said were training for an assault on the residence.

Newspapers are not allowed inside the residence in Peru's fashionable San Isidro district. But both the hostages and their captors listen to the radio, which reports extensively on what the newspapers say.
Security on the outskirts of the residence, where scores of journalists are camping out behind yellow police tapes, has been tightened since the arrest on Friday of three suspected guerrillas.
The arrests coincided with a decree that gave the police and army greater powers under an extension to all of Lima and the neighbouring port of Callao of a longstanding state of emergency.
At the same time, the Peruvian Congress voted by 82 to 0, with 8 abstentions, to give full support to Fujimori's refusal to compromise.
But Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages after Peru, stressed on Saturday that the crisis must be ended without loss of life.

"There is little advantage in reaching a compromise with terrorists, but a peaceful solution has become the key word in terms of preserving the lives of the captives," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters during his regular daily visit to a crisis room in the Foreign Ministry.
Fujimori, who has spoken only once in public since the crisis broke, has so far brushed aside outside offers of help.
